description: We are an aspiring AI and technology-driven team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 in cottbus. Our interests include Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Data Science, Space Exploration and solving real-world problems using innovative technology. We welcome passionate developers, designers, researchers and creative thinkers who want to collaborate, learn and build impactful solutions. Let’s turn ideas into innovation!
summary:
Ghost Explorers is an interactive 3D website where 18 machines NASA left behind on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space tell their own stories. Players can spin realistic 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, click on a spacecraft at its actual landing site, and meet pioneers like Surveyor 1, the Apollo moon rovers, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, and the Voyagers speaking in the first person.
Each machine shares its life in four short chapters including why I was sent, my journey, what I found, and where I am now. These are paired with a real NASA photo and a breakdown connecting its onboard tools to the science they made possible. At the end of each visit, players take a quick quiz to earn a passport stamp. Collecting all 18 stamps unlocks a completion certificate and opens up Level 2, inviting players to research another untold machine and write its story themselves.
By turning dense mission archives into personal stories for school age space fans, with every fact linked directly to its official NASA mission page, the project bridges the gap between raw data and human curiosity. Kids today mostly hear about the newest launches, while the trailblazing machines that made today’s discoveries possible are quietly forgotten. Ghost Explorers gives those machines a voice, and gives young explorers a reason to care.
details: Ghost Explorers is built around an immersive, hands-on experience. Instead of reading a page, users explore worlds: they drag to spin realistic 3D globes of the Moon and Mars, which keep gliding after release, and pinch or scroll to zoom in on the surface while live latitude and longitude readouts follow the cursor. Lighting from a fixed “Sun” casts a day–night edge across the cratered terrain, Mars glows with a soft atmospheric haze, and a field of 4,000 stars surrounds every scene. Each machine appears as a glowing, pulsing beacon at its real landing site. Selecting one turns the globe to face it, the camera zooms in, and the story slides in beside it, so the user feels they have travelled there. Every story unfolds chapter by chapter in the machine’s own voice, with optional read-aloud narration, real NASA photography and an instant quiz that stamps the user’s Explorer Passport, with a small celebratory note along the way. Completing all 18 reveals a personalized, printable certificate. The interface adapts to phones with a bottom-sheet layout and supports keyboard navigation and reduced-motion settings. Technically, it is a client-side web app (HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript) with three.js (WebGL) for real-time 3D, structured JavaScript data for the 18 stories, Python (fetch_images.py) for downloading the NASA images for offline use, and GitHub Pages for hosting. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to support development, and our team verified every fact against NASA sources.
